\n SO(3): Rotations and Infinitesimal Motion\n Rossmann · Ch 2.1\n

\n

SO(3)

\n
The Rotation Group
\n
\n A complicated curved group can be understood by studying its infinitesimal motions — its Lie algebra.\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Smartphone orientation
\n
Robot arm control
\n
3D graphics engines
\n
Aircraft attitude control
\n
\n
\n
\n \n
\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n
\n

This condition means the transformation preserves Euclidean geometry — lengths, angles, and dot products remain unchanged. It may rotate vectors, but never stretches or shrinks them.

\n
\n
\n
Preserves
\n
Lengths · Angles
Dot products · Orthogonality
\n
\n
\n
Equivalent to
\n
\n
Transpose exactly undoes the rotation
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — The Rigid Body
\n

Imagine rotating a rigid steel cube. Its shape never changes — every distance and angle inside stays the same. AᵀA = I is the mathematical statement of this: the transformation preserves all geometry. If it stretched anything, Aᵀ would not equal A⁻¹.

\n

\n
\n
\n

The Transpose

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n

The Inverse

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Bridge — Why These Two Are Connected
\n

The transpose \"reflects\" the matrix over its main diagonal. For a rotation matrix this reflection happens to reverse the rotation — but only because the columns are orthonormal. Not every matrix has this property.

The Column Proof

\n

Step through the proof that A⁻¹ = Aᵀ

\n
\n
Key Insight Before You Start
\n

Think of the columns of A as \"where the coordinate axes land after the rotation.\" Because a rotation is rigid, those new axis directions must still be unit vectors at right angles to each other — orthonormal. That orthonormality is the entire engine of the proof.

\n

Dot Product Proof

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Bridge — Two Proofs, One Truth
\n

The column proof asks \"what do the columns look like?\" — geometric. The dot product proof asks \"what does preserving inner products force?\" — algebraic. Both arrive at AᵀA = I from opposite angles.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

SO(3) as a Group

\n

Verifying all four group axioms for rotation matrices

\n
\n
\n
1. Closure — product of two rotations is a rotation
\n
\n
\n
\n
2. Identity — the identity matrix is in SO(3)
\n
\n
\n
\n
3. Inverses — every rotation has an inverse in SO(3)
\n
\n
\n
\n
4. Associativity — free from matrix multiplication
\n
(AB)C = A(BC) holds for all matrices — no verification needed.
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — Closure is the Key
\n

Composing two rotations gives another rotation — you can never \"escape\" SO(3) by rotating. This closure under composition is what makes it a group, not just a set of matrices.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

Non-Commutativity

\n
\n
\n
\n
The two matrices
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Order matters!
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — The Book Test
\n

Hold a book flat. Rotate it 90° around its spine (tilt it toward you), then 90° around the vertical axis. Now reset and do it the other way: vertical first, then spine. You get a different orientation. This is why SO(3) is a non-abelian group — the order of operations matters.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

Why Does This Matter?

\n

Real systems where SO(3) is the backbone

\n
\n
\n
Smartphone Orientation
\n

Your phone's gyroscope tracks 3D orientation as an element of SO(3). Since A⁻¹ = Aᵀ, rotation inversion is just a transpose — near-zero compute cost.

\n
\n
\n
Robotics
\n

The orientation of a robot arm's end-effector lives in SO(3). The non-commutativity of rotations is crucial — planning must track the exact order of joint rotations.

\n
\n
\n
3D Graphics
\n

Every rotating object in a game or film uses a rotation matrix. Graphics hardware is optimised around the orthogonality structure of SO(3) matrices — millions of matrix products per second.

\n
\n
\n
Flight and Spacecraft
\n

Pitch, roll, and yaw are elements of the Lie algebra of SO(3). The full 3D attitude of an aircraft is an element of SO(3). Non-commutativity matters: yaw-then-pitch ≠ pitch-then-yaw.

\n
\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Pure rotation. Orientation-preserving.
\n
\n
\n
\n
Reflection or improper rotation. Not in SO(3).
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — Handedness
\n

Hold up your right hand. A pure rotation (det = +1) preserves handedness — the orientation of space stays the same. A reflection (det = −1) flips it: your right hand becomes a left hand. SO(3) lives entirely in the orientation-preserving half of the orthogonal group O(3).

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

Axis-Angle Representation

\n
\n

Every rotation is determined by a unit axis vector and an angle. This gives the Rodrigues rotation formula:

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — Every Rotation is Simple
\n

No matter how you combine rotations — no matter how complex the sequence — the net effect is always just a single rotation around one axis by one angle. The Rodrigues formula makes that axis and angle explicit. This is Euler's remarkable theorem.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

The Lie Algebra so(3)

\n

Infinitesimal rotations — the tangent space at the identity

\n
\n

This is a 3-dimensional real vector space. The connection to SO(3): if we differentiate a smooth path of rotation matrices through the identity, we get a skew-symmetric matrix. Conversely, every skew-symmetric matrix arises this way.

\n
\n
\n
\n
The Lie Bracket (Commutator)
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — Linearizing Rotations
\n

The Lie algebra captures rotations \"near the identity\" — infinitely small rotations. These form a simple flat vector space, much easier than the curved manifold SO(3). The commutation relations [L₁, L₂] = L₃ encode the same non-commutativity of rotations, now algebraically. The isomorphism so(3) ≅ ℝ³ is why angular velocity is a vector.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

Lemma 1B: The Axis-Plane Shape

\n

A finite rotation and an infinitesimal rotation have the same hidden geometry.

\n

Rossmann's Lemma 1B says that every element of SO(3) can be viewed, in the right orthonormal basis, as an ordinary planar rotation plus one fixed axis. The Lie algebra version says the same thing infinitesimally: every skew-symmetric matrix rotates one perpendicular plane and kills one axis direction.

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Why a fixed axis exists
\n
\n
\n
\n
Why the plane is preserved
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — 3D rotation is secretly 2D
\n

A rotation in three dimensions looks complicated only because the axis may be tilted. Once you choose the axis as one basis vector, the whole problem collapses to the familiar two-dimensional cosine-sine block. The perpendicular plane spins; the axis stays still. The infinitesimal matrix has the same split, except the cosine-sine block has been replaced by its velocity at time zero.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

The Cross Product Hiding Inside so(3)

\n

The hat map translates angular-velocity vectors into skew-symmetric matrices.

\n

The cross product is not an extra trick bolted onto SO(3). It is the vector-language version of the Lie algebra. If \\(\\omega\\) is angular velocity and \\(r\\) is the position of a point, then \\(\\omega\\times r\\) is the instantaneous velocity of that point.

\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Sideways velocity is the main idea
\n
\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — why the bracket becomes a cross product
\n

Tiny rotations about two different axes do not quite cancel when you swap their order. The leftover infinitesimal rotation points in the cross-product direction. That is why \\([\\widehat{x},\\widehat{y}]=\\widehat{x\\times y}\\): the matrix commutator and the vector cross product are the same rotational non-commutativity written in two dialects.

\n
\n
\n\n \n
\n

The Exponential Map

\n

The exponential map is the bridge between the Lie algebra and the group. It sends skew-symmetric matrices to rotation matrices:

\n
\n

Because skew-symmetric matrices satisfy a special identity (K³ = −K for unit K), the infinite series collapses to a closed form identical to the Rodrigues formula:

\n
\n
\n
\n
Intuition — Flowing Along the Algebra
\n

Think of B ∈ so(3) as a \"direction to rotate\" and t as time. The path eᵗᴮ is a smooth curve through the group starting at the identity and flowing in direction B. The exponential map is the operation of following this flow for unit time — turning an infinitesimal rotation into a finite one.

The Big Picture

\n

SO(3) is a Lie group: simultaneously a smooth 3-dimensional curved manifold and an algebraic group. Every point on this manifold is a rotation matrix.

\n

Rossmann's central idea: study the tangent space at the identity — the Lie algebra so(3) — which is flat, linear, and easy to work with. The exponential map carries you from the algebra back to the group:

\n
\n
\n
Complete Summary
\n
    \n
  1. SO(3) is the group of all 3×3 rotation matrices: AᵀA = I and det(A) = 1.
    2. \n
  2. AᵀA = I preserves lengths, angles, and dot products.
    3. \n
  3. The columns of A form an orthonormal basis → A⁻¹ = Aᵀ.
    4. \n
  4. det(A) = 1 selects rotations, excluding reflections (det = −1).
    5. \n
  5. SO(3) is a non-abelian group: AB ≠ BA in general.
    6. \n
  6. By Euler's theorem, every rotation is rotation around some axis by some angle.
    7. \n
  7. The Rodrigues formula parametrizes this: R = cos θ · I + sin θ · [n̂]× + (1 − cos θ) n̂n̂ᵀ.
    8. \n
  8. The Lie algebra so(3) = {skew-symmetric matrices} is the tangent space at I.
    9. \n
  9. Generators L₁, L₂, L₃ satisfy [Lᵢ, Lⱼ] = εᵢⱼₖ Lₖ — encoding the non-commutativity.
    10. \n
  10. The exponential map exp: so(3) → SO(3) sends every infinitesimal rotation to a finite one.
    11. \n
  11. Lemma 1B explains why this works: both finite and infinitesimal rotations reduce to one fixed axis plus a rotating perpendicular plane.
    12. \n
  12. The hat map turns angular velocity into a skew matrix, and the Lie bracket becomes the ordinary cross product.
    13. \n
\n

Related reading: The Engine & the Motion develops the general exponential-map intuition, and Vector Products explains the dot, cross, and wedge viewpoints that sit behind the geometry here.

This measures how much two infinitesimal rotations fail to commute.');\n this._set('math-la5','\\\\[[L_1,L_2]=L_3,\\\\qquad[L_2,L_3]=L_1,\\\\qquad[L_3,L_1]=L_2\\\\] In terms of angular velocity: \\\\([\\\\omega,\\\\eta]_\\\\times = \\\\omega\\\\times\\\\eta\\\\) — the Lie bracket corresponds to the cross product on \\\\(\\\\mathbb{R}^3\\\\).');\n // Lemma 1B and axis-plane form\n this._set('math-lemma1','Finite rotation form: for every \\(A\\in SO(3)\\), there is a right-handed orthonormal basis \\(e_1,e_2,e_3\\) and an angle \\(\\alpha\\) such that\\[Ae_1=\\cos\\alpha\\,e_1+\\sin\\alpha\\,e_2,\\quad Ae_2=-\\sin\\alpha\\,e_1+\\cos\\alpha\\,e_2,\\quad Ae_3=e_3.\\]Equivalently, in that basis,\\[[A]=\\begin{bmatrix}\\cos\\alpha&-\\sin\\alpha&0\\\\sin\\alpha&\\cos\\alpha&0\\0&0&1\\end{bmatrix}.\\]');\n this._set('math-lemma2','Infinitesimal form: for every \\(X\\in\\mathfrak{so}(3)\\), there is a right-handed orthonormal basis \\(e_1,e_2,e_3\\) and a real number \\(\\alpha\\) such that\\[Xe_1=\\alpha e_2,\\quad Xe_2=-\\alpha e_1,\\quad Xe_3=0,\\qquad [X]=\\begin{bmatrix}0&-\\alpha&0\\\\alpha&0&0\\0&0&0\\end{bmatrix}.\\]');\n this._set('math-lemma3','The exponential connects the two normal forms. Since \\(J=\\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\\end{bmatrix}\\) satisfies \\(J^2=-I\\),\\[e^{\\alpha J}=\\cos\\alpha\\,I+\\sin\\alpha\\,J.\\]So exponentiating the infinitesimal block gives exactly the finite rotation block.');\n this._set('math-axiswhy','A real \\(3\\times3\\) matrix has at least one real eigenvalue. If \\(Av=\\lambda v\\) and \\(A\\) is orthogonal, then \\(\\|Av\\|=\\|v\\|\\), so \\(|\\lambda|=1\\). The non-real eigenvalues occur as a conjugate pair with product 1, and \\(\\det A=1\\) forces the remaining real eigenvalue to be \\(+1\\). Thus some nonzero vector satisfies \\(Ae_3=e_3\\).');\n this._set('math-planewhy','Let \\(P=e_3^\\perp\\). If \\(v\\in P\\), then \\(\\langle v,e_3\\rangle=0\\). Since \\(A\\) preserves inner products and \\(Ae_3=e_3\\),\\[\\langle Av,e_3\\rangle=\\langle Av,Ae_3\\rangle=\\langle v,e_3\\rangle=0.\\]So \\(Av\\in P\\): the plane perpendicular to the axis is invariant.');\n // Cross product and hat map\n this._set('math-cross1','For \\(\\omega=(\\omega_1,\\omega_2,\\omega_3)^T\\), define the hat map\\[\\widehat{\\omega}=\\begin{bmatrix}0&-\\omega_3&\\omega_2\\\\omega_3&0&-\\omega_1\\-\\omega_2&\\omega_1&0\\end{bmatrix}.\\]Then \\(\\widehat{\\omega}v=\\omega\\times v\\). This is the concrete identification \\(\\mathbb{R}^3\\cong\\mathfrak{so}(3)\\).');\n this._set('math-cross2','Example: for \\(\\omega=e_3\\),\\[\\widehat{\\omega}=\\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0\\end{bmatrix},\\quad \\widehat{\\omega}e_1=e_2,\\quad \\widehat{\\omega}e_2=-e_1,\\quad \\widehat{\\omega}e_3=0.\\]These are exactly \\(e_3\\times e_1=e_2\\), \\(e_3\\times e_2=-e_1\\), and \\(e_3\\times e_3=0\\).');\n this._set('math-cross3','The dynamic meaning is\\[\\dot r=\\omega\\times r=\\widehat{\\omega}r.\\]If \\(\\omega=\\omega e_3\\) and \\(r=e_1\\), then \\(\\omega\\times r=\\omega e_2\\): a point on the positive x-axis initially moves in the positive y-direction under a positive z-axis rotation.');\n this._set('math-sideways','For any skew-symmetric \\(X\\),\\[\\langle Xv,v\\rangle=-\\langle v,Xv\\rangle.\\]Over the real numbers the two inner products are equal, so \\(\\langle Xv,v\\rangle=0\\). Thus \\(Xv\\perp v\\). A skew matrix does not push a vector along itself; it pushes it sideways. Sideways instantaneous velocity is what produces circular motion rather than stretching.');\n this._set('math-cross4','The bracket-cross-product dictionary is\\[[\\widehat{x},\\widehat{y}]=\\widehat{x\\times y}.\\]For instance, \\(e_1\\times e_2=e_3\\), so the commutator of tiny x-axis and y-axis rotations is a tiny z-axis rotation.');\n // Exponential map\n this._set('math-exp1','\\\\[\\\\exp:\\\\mathfrak{so}(3)\\\\to SO(3),\\\\quad B\\\\mapsto e^B=\\\\sum_{k=0}^{\\\\infty}\\\\frac{B^k}{k!}=I+B+\\\\frac{B^2}{2!}+\\\\cdots\\\\]');\n this._set('math-exp2','For \\\\(B=\\\\theta K\\\\) where \\\\(K\\\\) is unit skew-symmetric (satisfying \\\\(K^3=-K\\\\)), the series reduces to:\\\\[e^{\\\\theta K}=I+\\\\sin(\\\\theta)K+(1-\\\\cos\\\\theta)K^2\\\\] — the same as the Rodrigues formula.');\n this._set('math-exp3','This is the bridge between the Lie algebra and the group: every rotation matrix \\(A\\in SO(3)\\) arises as \\(e^B\\) for some \\(B\\in\\mathfrak{so}(3)\\). The exponential map is surjective: Lemma 1B puts every rotation into a planar block, and the planar block is \\(e^{\\alpha J}\\). It is not injective, because adding full turns gives the same rotation: \\(e^{\\alpha\\widehat u}=e^{(\\alpha+2\\pi k)\\widehat u}\\).');\n // Big picture\n this._set('math-bigpic','\\\\[\\\\mathfrak{so}(3)\\\\xrightarrow{\\\\;\\\\exp\\\\;}SO(3),\\\\qquad B\\\\mapsto e^B\\\\]');\n this._updateProof();\n this._updateCard();\n }\n\n _updateProof(){\n const
